evidence.quote: Ni-based superalloys are based on the precipitation strengthening of the Ni3Al-based γ'-phase particles in an face centered cubic Ni-based γ-matrix phase.

LEK94, a rhenium-containing single crystal superalloy with a low density between 8.1 and 8.3 g cm−3, was developed by MTU Aero Engines, München, Germany.
The second-generation nickel-based single crystal superalloy MC2 was developed by ONERA in the late 1980s.
CMSX-10 is a third-generation single-crystal alloy, developed by Cannon-Muskegon for a temperature range of 850–950 °C, and is, e.g., used in the Rolls-Royce engine TRENT 800.

The specific heat capacity of liquid LEK94 (cp = 0.749 ± 0.006 J (g K)⁻¹, between 1550 and 1850 K) corresponds well to the value obtained by Amore et al. [51] in a ground-based differential scanning calorimeter of 0.75 J(g K)⁻¹, with an estimated error of ±10% in the temperature range of 1650–1750 K.
The specific heat capacity of MC2 (0.67 ± 0.05 J(g K)⁻¹) is only 5% higher than the prediction by Kopp–Neumann rule (0.635 J(g K)⁻¹).

The specific heat capacity of CMSX-10 is given as 0.63 J (g K)⁻¹ without measurement uncertainty by Quested et al. [54], which is only 11% below the value of (0.71 ± 0.05) J(gK)⁻¹ determined in our study.
The specific resistivity of LEK94 obtained from the dedicated measurement cycles is found to be 138 μΩ·cm in the stable and undercooled liquid phase, without significant temperature dependence.
